result: The authors developed an open-top two-photon light sheet microscopy (OT-TP-LSM) system that integrates open-top configuration with two-photon excitation using a scanned Bessel beam to generate an extended depth of field light sheet. The system achieved high-speed imaging at 400 fps with 0.24 mm²/s throughput, 0.9 μm resolution in all dimensions, and a field of view of 600 μm × 170 μm.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly acknowledge the development and integration of OT-TP-LSM. The editor states this is 'important work' demonstrating the technique. Reviewer 1 notes 'this is the first system of integrating the two' (open-top LSM and two-photon microscopy). Reviewer 2 confirms 'high-speed and high-depth imaging' with the stated specifications. The technical implementation details are accepted without challenge.

result: OT-TP-LSM achieved improved imaging depth compared to single-photon excitation methods. In skin tissue, the system reached ~64 μm actual depth (90 μm in 45° tilted plane), approximately three times deeper than conventional one-photon LSM (~20 μm). Using propidium iodide (PI) instead of proflavine in pancreas specimens increased imaging depth from ~30 μm to ~55 μm due to longer emission wavelength.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly highlights 'the integration provides better imaging depth than a single-photon excitation OT-LSM' as a key strength. Reviewer 1 also notes 'Use of propidium iodide (PI) provided a deeper imaging depth' as a strength. Reviewer 2 confirms the achievement of 'high-depth imaging' and the depth specifications. The comparative advantage over single-photon methods is accepted without question.

result: OT-TP-LSM successfully visualized 3D cellular structures and extracellular matrix (ECM) via SHG in human skin cancer specimens, including basal cell carcinoma (BCC). The system distinguished BCC tumor nests from normal glandular structures (eccrine and sebaceous glands) in the dermis, which could appear similar in 2D images. The 3D visualization capability enhanced cancer detection and differentiation.
evaluation: The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique investigating various human cancer cells.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'This was confirmed by 3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate.' The ability to distinguish normal from cancerous structures is implicitly accepted through the reviewers' acknowledgment of the technique's effectiveness for cancer cell investigation.

result: OT-TP-LSM visualized normal and premalignant pancreatic tissue structures, including acini, islets of Langerhans, ducts, and precursor lesions (IPMN and PanIN). The images showed good correlation with H&E histology and provided comparable histopathological information without thin sectioning. Pancreatic cancers were clearly identified using 3D visualization.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'This was confirmed by 3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate.' The editor's statement that the authors provide 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique' encompasses the pancreatic imaging results. No reviewer challenges the quality or interpretation of the pancreatic tissue imaging.

result: OT-TP-LSM visualized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) arising from IPMN, showing irregularly shaped cancer glands with 3D structural complexity, disorganized cell arrangement, and desmoplastic stroma. The system distinguished cancer glands from nonneoplastic ducts and visualized 3D invasiveness that could not be identified from 2D information.
evaluation: This result is encompassed within Reviewer 2's confirmation of successful '3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate' and the editor's statement about 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique.' The detailed characterization of PDAC features is not challenged by any reviewer.

result: OT-TP-LSM successfully imaged benign and malignant prostate tissue, distinguishing benign glands with multiple cell layers from cancer glands with single-layered cells due to loss of basal cell layers. The system provided histological 3D information equivalent to H&E stained images without sectioning for Gleason score 3+3 prostatic adenocarcinoma.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'This was confirmed by 3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate.' The editor's endorsement of 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique' includes the prostate imaging results. No concerns are raised about the prostate tissue characterization.

result: An unsupervised deep learning network (CycleGAN) was employed to convert OT-TP-LSM images to virtual H&E images. The virtual H&E images of PanIN and PDAC showed similar patterns to real H&E histology and displayed diagnostic features for discriminating cancer types. However, some regions were not transformed properly, and further development is needed for robust performance.
evaluation: While no reviewer explicitly discusses the CycleGAN results in detail, the overall acceptance of the work as 'important' (editor) and providing 'convincing evidence' implicitly includes this component. The authors' own acknowledgment of limitations (improper transformation of some regions, need for further development) is presented transparently and does not elicit reviewer criticism, suggesting acceptance of the proof-of-concept demonstration.

result: The liquid prism design minimized aberration through refractive index matching, though spherical aberration from RI mismatch between air and immersion medium degraded lateral resolution in the Y-Z' plane to ~128% of theoretical value. This resolution was still sufficient for detecting cellular features.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly identifies 'Use of liquid prism to minimize the aberration induced by index mismatching' as 'interesting and potentially helpful to other researchers in the field.' The acknowledgment of residual aberration and its limited impact on cellular detection is not challenged, indicating acceptance of this technical trade-off.

result: The imaging depth of OT-TP-LSM was sufficient for visualizing 3D cell structures in skin without sectioning artifacts, though relatively low compared to conventional point-scanning TPM due to emission photon scattering. Imaging depth varied by tissue type, with pancreas and prostate showing lower depths than skin, attributed to dense cell composition and higher refractive index.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms the achievement of 'high-depth imaging' and notes the system achieved 'An extended depth of field of 180 µm in 0.9 µm thickness.' The comparative limitation versus conventional TPM and tissue-dependent variation are presented as technical realities rather than fundamental flaws, and no reviewer challenges these characterizations.

result: OT-TP-LSM may have potential for histopathological examination in surgical and biopsy applications by rapidly providing 3D information as a complement to traditional H&E pathology, offering nondestructive 3D pathology capabilities.
evaluation: The editor characterizes this as 'important work' for 'lesser invasive evaluation of intraoperative 3D pathology' and states 'This article will be of broad interest to biologists and, specifically, pathologists utilizing 3D optical microscopy.' Reviewer 2 notes the data shows 'OT-T-LSM could be a complementary technique to traditional imaging workflows.' The potential application is endorsed by reviewers.

result: Post-processing time of OT-TP-LSM image datasets was relatively long due to large data size, sequential processing, and manual stitching. This needs to be resolved for intraoperative applications, with suggestions including FPGA-based acquisition, GPU computing, C++ coding, and automatic stitching software.
evaluation: No reviewer raises concerns about the processing time limitation or challenges the proposed solutions. The transparent acknowledgment of this limitation and discussion of potential solutions is implicitly accepted. The lack of reviewer criticism suggests this is viewed as an addressable technical challenge rather than a fundamental flaw.
